content.content:
parameter type of the other.  In this case, there is no possibility of
ambiguous calls, because one declaration is more specific than the
other.  This section also places a restriction on the return types of
the overloaded declarations to ensure that type safety is not
violated.  \secref{incompatibility-rule} defines the \emph{
Incompatibility Rule} that, if satisfied by a pair of declarations,
guarantees that neither declaration is applicable to the same
functional call.  In \secref{more-specific-rule}, the \emph{Meet Rule}
requires the existence of a declaration that is more specific than
both overloaded declarations in the situation that both are applicable
to a given call.

In the remainder of this chapter, we build on the terminology and
notation defined in \chapref{multiple-dispatch}
and \chapref{conversions-coercions}.



\section{Subtype Rule}
\seclabel{subtype-rule}

If the parameter type of one declaration is a subtype of the parameter
type of another (and they are not the same) then there is no
ambiguity between these two declarations: for every call to which both
are applicable, the first is more specific.  This is the basis of the
Subtype Rule.

The Subtype Rule also requires a relationship between the return types
of the two declarations.  Without such a requirement, a program may
violate type safety.

\paragraph{The Subtype Rule for Functions and Functional Methods:}
Suppose that $\f(\Ps) : \Us$ and $\f(\Qs) : \Vs$ are two distinct
function or functional method declarations in a single scope.
If $\Ps \strictsubtype \Qs$ and $\Us \Ovrsubtype \Vs$ then $\f(\Ps)$ and
$\f(\Qs)$ are a valid overloading.

\paragraph{The Subtype Rule for Dotted Methods:}
Suppose that $\Ps_0.\f(\Ps) : \Us$ and $\Qs_0.\f(\Qs) : \Vs$ are two
distinct dotted method declarations provided by a trait or object $C$.
If $\Ps_0 \strictsubtype \Qs_0$, $\Ps \strictsubtype \Qs$,
and $\Us \Ovrsubtype
\Vs$ then $\Ps_0.\f(\Ps)$ and $\Qs_0.\f(\Qs)$ are a valid overloading.

\section{Incompatibility Rule}
\seclabel{incompatibility-rule}

The basic idea behind the Incompatibility Rule is that if there is no
call to which two overloaded declarations are both applicable
then there is no potential for ambiguous calls.  In such a case, we say
that the declarations are incompatible.
Without coercion, incompatibility is equivalent to exclusion.
However, the presence of coercion complicates the definition of
incompatibility.  To formally define incompatibility we first define the
following notation.
%
For types $T$ and $U$,
we say that $T$ and $U$ \emph{do not share coercions}, and write
$T \noshare U$, if any type that coerces to $T$ excludes any type
that coerces to $U$:
\[
T \noshare U \iff \forall A,B: A \coercedefto T \logicand B \coercedefto U
                               \implies A \excludes B.
\]
%
We say that $T$ \emph{is incompatible with} $U$, and write $T
\incompatible U$, if $T$ and $U$ exclude, reject each other, and do
not share coercions:
\begin{align*}
T \incompatible U \iff
&T \excludes U \logicand T \rejects U \logicand U \rejects T \logicand  T \noshare U \\
\iff
&\phantom{\logicand\ } T \excludes U \\
&\logicand\ (\forall A: A \coercedefto T \implies A \excludes U) \\
&\logicand\ (\forall B: B \coercedefto U \implies B \excludes T) \\
&\logicand\ (\forall A,B: A \coercedefto T \logicand B \coercedefto U
                          \implies A \excludes B)
\end{align*}
Note that if $T \incompatible U$ then no type is substitutable for
both $T$ and $U$.

\paragraph{The Incompatibility Rule for Functions and Functional Methods:}

Suppose that $\f(\Ps)$ and $\f(\Qs)$ are two distinct function or
functional method declarations in a single scope.
If $\Ps \incompatible \Qs$ then $\f(\Ps)$ and $\f(\Qs)$ are a valid overloading.

\paragraph{The Incompatibility Rule for Dotted Methods:}
Suppose that $\Ps_0.\f(\Ps)$ and $\Qs_0.\f(\Qs)$ are two distinct
dotted method declarations provided by a trait or object $C$.  If
$\Ps \incompatible \Qs$ then $\Ps_0.\f(\Ps)$ and $\Qs_0.\f(\Qs)$ are
a valid overloading.

\section{Meet Rule}
\seclabel{more-specific-rule}

If neither the Subtype Rule nor the Incompatibility Rule holds 
for a pair of overloaded declarations 
then the declarations introduce the possibility of ambiguity.  
To avoid this ambiguity, 
we require a \emph{disambiguating declaration}:
for any possible arguments to which both declarations are applicable, 
there must be another more specific declaration that is also applicable.  
Thus, 
if the functional is called with such arguments, 
neither of the pair of declarations is executed 
because the disambiguating declaration is also applicable, 
and it is more specific than both.

\note{What is "an intersection of two declarations"?
-- Sukyoung

For function declarations we require that the disambiguating
declaration be the intersection of the pair of overloaded
declarations.}

\paragraph{The Meet Rule for Functions:}
Suppose that $\f(\Ps)$ and $\f(\Qs)$ are two function
declarations in a single scope
such that neither $\Ps$ nor $\Qs$ is a subtype of the other and $\Ps$ and
$\Qs$ are not incompatible with one another.
Let $\mathpzc{S}$ be the set of types that $\Ps$ defines coercions from
and $\mathpzc{T}$ be the set of types that $\Qs$ defines coercions from.
$\f(\Ps)$ and $\f(\Qs)$ are a valid overloading if
there is a declaration $\f(\Ps \inter \Qs)$ in the scope.

all of the following hold:
\begin{itemize}
\item
either $\Ps \excludes \Qs$ or there is a declaration $\f(\Ps \inter
\Qs)$ in the scope,

+proofs of correctness'' (Park, Hong, Steele and Ryu, POPL 2019, Sections~5.2
+and~5.4).
+Naden's notes of 2012 on instantiation at run time restricted by the return type
+(\nolinkurl{Papers/RuntimeInstantiation/}, in the revival's repository) are the
+type group's draft of that rule; the type group's paper of 2011 left the
+run-time inference of the static arguments of a dispatched declaration ``beyond
+the scope of this paper'' (\nolinkurl{Papers/Types/rules.tick}, lines 118--129).
+The paper's dispatcher solves every call so; this text keeps the instance
+inferred for the declaration that the static call selected, which differs from
+the paper's only for a type parameter that neither the static type of the call
+nor an invariant position in a parameter type constrains.
+The full reasoning is in
+\nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-spec-overloading/decision-record.md}
+in the revival's repository.
+\item[Effect] No value that a valid program computes changes.
+The interpreter, which has no static types, and the compiled path, whose
+dispatcher is not given the static type of the call, take the dynamic type of
+the argument where the value does not fix the type parameter; the compiled
+path's departure is gated as an expected failure (row~NNN of the revival's gap
+ledger).
+The compiled path does not yet run a generic declaration that a call reaches
+only by dispatch beside a plain one (row~496).
+The instance of a \KWD{nat} or \KWD{int} parameter that nothing fixes at run
+time is not described (\secref{revival-notrevised}).
+\item[Original text] The paragraph is unchanged:
+\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/overloading.tex}, lines 263--276:
+\begin{quote}
+To evaluate a given functional call, it is necessary to determine which
+functional declaration to dispatch to.
+To do so, we consider the declarations that are applicable to that call at run
+time.
+If there is exactly one such declaration, then the call dispatches to that
+declaration.
+If there is no such declaration, then the call is \emph{undefined}, which is a
+static error.
+(However, see \secref{applicability-with-coercion} for how coercion may add to
+the set of applicable declarations.)
+If multiple declarations are applicable to the call at run time, then we choose
+an arbitrary declaration among the declarations such that no other applicable
+declaration is more specific than them.
+\end{quote}
+The Working Draft forbade both pairs of the examples, by its lines 100--105,
+quoted in \secref{revival-overloading}.
+\item[Route C] The same under route~C.
+\end{description}
+
+\subsection{The interpreter's choice of a coercion}
+\seclabel{revival-coercion-walk}
+
+\begin{description}
+\item[Affected section] \secref{resolving-coercion}.
+\item[Change] One box after the example of the paragraph that says that
+coercion is resolved statically; the paragraph and its example are unchanged.
+The box says that the compiled path follows the text; that the interpreter,
+which has no static types, chooses a coercion on the value and so runs
+\EXP{f(B)} for the example's \EXP{f(c)}, and answers the same way wherever an
+argument's value is of a type that another declaration already fits; that both
+cases are gated as expected failures; and that the interpreter is to follow the
+text once it takes the coercions that the compiled type checker inserts.
+\item[Rationale] This change does not follow from route~A; the revival decided
+on 29~September 2026 that the interpreter's choice of a coercion on the value is
+its limit, since it has no static types from which to resolve a coercion
+statically, and that the interpreter is made to follow the text once the
+compiled type checker checks the programs it runs and it takes the coercions the
+checker inserts.
+The type group's paper of 2019 also carries the static types of calls to run
+time for its dispatcher, which the interpreter does not have.
+\item[Effect] None on the language.
+The interpreter's answer, 4 where the text gives 3, and its answer in the
+narrower case are gated by
+\nolinkurl{ProjectFortress/tests/XXXCoercionStaticRungC.fss} and
+\nolinkurl{ProjectFortress/tests/XXXCoercionStaticNarrowRungC.fss} (row~19 of
+the revival's gap ledger).
+\item[Original text] The passage is unchanged:
+\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/conversions-coercions.tex}, lines
+567--604, which begin:
+\begin{quote}
+Notice that coercion is resolved statically.  Once a coercion is statically
+chosen for a call, this coercion is conceptually inserted into the call.
+This means that the statically chosen coercion is applied at run time.
+\end{quote}
+\item[Route C] The same under route~C.
+\end{description}
+
+\subsection{Traits with comprises clauses read at the level of values}
+\seclabel{revival-covering}
+
+\begin{description}
+\item[Affected sections] \secref{internal-types};
+\secref{abstractFunctionDeclarations}; a draft note in the subsection ``Export
+Statements'' of \secref{components}; the effect of \secref{revival-comprises}.
+\item[Change] \secref{internal-types} defines covering: a type covers another
+when every value of the second is a value of the first; a type covers each of
+its subtypes, and a trait with a \KWD{comprises} clause is covered by the union
+of its listed types; covering is not the subtype relation.
+Its example concludes that $V$ covers $S \inter T$, where it concluded that
+$V = S \inter T$, and a sentence says that a trait may stand between $S$ or $T$
+and their listed types, so that $S \inter T$ is not in general equal to a named
+type.
+\secref{abstractFunctionDeclarations} asks the argument types of the concrete
+declarations to cover the argument type of the abstract declaration, where it
+asked their union to equal it, and, in its example, for a definition for every
+type listed in the \KWD{comprises} clause of \TYP{Molecule} or definitions that
+together cover those types, where it asked for one for every immediate subtype.
+Each of these four passages has a box.
+The draft note says ``all its listed types'' where it said ``all its immediate
+subtraits''; a draft note prints only in a draft build, so it has no box.

#!/bin/bash
# Run one probe on both paths, each in a private cache.
#   run-probe.sh <probe-dir> <Name> <scratch> <libcache>
# walk:     bin/fortress <Name>.fss, caches in <scratch>/<Name>/walk
# compiled: bin/fortress compile <Name>.fss into a copy of <libcache> (the compiler's
#           library components already compiled there), then MainWrapper <Name>.
# Prints the two transcripts, bounded, with their exit codes.
set -u
PD=$1 ; N=$2 ; S=$3 ; L=$4
FH=${FORTRESS_HOME:?}
W=$S/$N/walk ; C=$S/$N/comp
rm -rf "$S/$N" ; mkdir -p "$W" ; cp -r "$L" "$C"
CP=$("$FH/bin/fortress_classpath")
cd "$PD"
echo "### walk: bin/fortress $N.fss"
JAVA_FLAGS="$JAVA_FLAGS -Dfortress.caches=$W" timeout 600 "$FH/bin/fortress" "$N.fss" > "$S/$N/walk.txt" 2>&1 ; echo "### walk rc=$?"
head -c 3000 "$S/$N/walk.txt" | sed "s|$FH/||g; s|$PD/||g"
echo "### compile: bin/fortress compile $N.fss"
JAVA_FLAGS="$JAVA_FLAGS -Dfortress.caches=$C" timeout 600 "$FH/bin/fortress" compile "$N.fss" > "$S/$N/compile.txt" 2>&1 ; echo "### compile rc=$?"
head -c 3000 "$S/$N/compile.txt" | sed "s|$FH/||g; s|$PD/||g"
if [ -f "$C/bytecode_cache/$N.jar" ] ; then
  echo "### run: MainWrapper $N"
  timeout 600 java -Xss64m -cp "$C/bytecode_cache:$C/bytecode_cache/*:$C/nativewrapper_cache:$CP" com.sun.fortress.runtimeSystem.MainWrapper "$N" > "$S/$N/run.txt" 2>&1 ; echo "### run rc=$?"
  head -c 3000 "$S/$N/run.txt" | sed "s|$FH/||g; s|$PD/||g"
else
  echo "### run: no $N.jar produced"
fi

+subtraits''; a draft note prints only in a draft build, so it has no box.
+The effect of \secref{revival-comprises} no longer says that these passages are
+not revised.
+\item[Rationale] This change does not follow from route~A; the revival decided
+on 29~September 2026 that the passages that read a \KWD{comprises} clause at the
+level of types are restated at the level of values, which is how
+\secref{trait-decls} reads the clause since its revision of 28~September 2026
+(\secref{revival-comprises}).
+The team's later Types chapter names covering beside subtyping and exclusion as
+a relation between types, and says that an instantiation of a trait with a
+\KWD{comprises} clause ``is covered by the union'' of the listed types
+(\nolinkurl{Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick}, lines 36--38
+and 384--390, in the revival's repository).
+Welterweight Fortress, the type group's calculus of 2012, reads the clause at
+the level of values and counts an abstract declaration as covered when it is
+implemented for all the types comprised
+(\nolinkurl{Papers/Welterweight/grammar.tick}, lines 21--22;
+\nolinkurl{Papers/Welterweight/fig-covered.tick}).
+Under that reading a trait with static parameters may stand unlisted between a
+trait with a \KWD{comprises} clause and its listed types; an instantiation of it
+is then a subtype of the closed trait and of no listed type, though every value
+of it is a value of a listed type, so the passages' conclusions hold of values
+and not of types.
+The full reasoning is in
+\nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-spec-overloading/decision-record.md}
+and \nolinkurl{explorations/reviews/comprises-type-level-judgement.md} in the
+revival's repository.
+\item[Effect] No example of this specification becomes invalid.
+Covering is not subtyping: where an instantiation of a trait with static
+parameters stands between $S$ and $T$ and their listed types, its value is a
+value of $V$ but its static type is not a subtype of $V$, and the compiled type
+checker refuses to assign it to a variable of type $V$; the interpreter, which
+has no static types, runs such an assignment.
+The compiled type checker checks the abstract methods of a trait with a
+\KWD{comprises} clause for definitions on its listed types; top-level abstract
+function declarations run on neither implementation.
+\item[Original text] \nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/types-vals-vars.tex},
+lines 568--570:
+\begin{quote}
+because of the \KWD{comprises} clauses of $S$ and $T$ and the \KWD{excludes}
+clause of $U$, any subtype of both $S$ and $T$ must be a subtype of $V$.  Thus,
+$V = S \inter T$.
+\end{quote}
+\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/functions.tex}, lines 377--378:
+\begin{quote}
+Furthermore, the union of the argument types of the concrete declarations for
+\VAR{f} must be equal to \VAR{T}.
+\end{quote}
+and lines 413--415:
+\begin{quote}
+For the latter, the programmer must provide a definition for every immediate
+subtype of \TYP{Molecule}, or it is a static error.
+\end{quote}
+\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/components/source-code.tex}, line
+429, the words of the draft note's second item that changed:
+\begin{quote}
+provided that all its immediate subtraits are considered to have concrete
+method declaration with that signature.
+\end{quote}
+The effect of \secref{revival-comprises}, the revival's text of 28~September
+2026, ended:
+\begin{quote}
+The passages that read a \KWD{comprises} clause at the level of types, the
+intersection of two traits with such clauses (\secref{internal-types},
+\secref{more-specific-rule}) and the definitions an abstract function
+declaration requires (\secref{abstractFunctionDeclarations}), are not revised;
+whether they are to be restated at the level of values is not settled.
+\end{quote}
+\item[Route C] The same under route~C: the reading of a \KWD{comprises} clause
+at the level of values does not depend on the rule on instantiations.
+\end{description}
+
+\subsection{The Meet Rule for traits with comprises clauses}
+\seclabel{revival-meet}
+
+\begin{description}
+\item[Affected sections] \secref{principles-overloading};
+\secref{more-specific-rule}; \secref{overloading-static-params};
+\secref{overloading-coercion-resolution}; and, in a draft build, the proposed
+features of the appendix ``Internal Document''.
+\item[Change] Where the Meet Rule for functions, or for functional methods,
+asks for a declaration on the intersection of two parameter types, declarations
+whose parameter types are each a subtype of both and together cover the
+intersection also satisfy it, every pair of those declarations satisfying the
+rules in turn; the case does not apply to the condition on the types from which
+the two parameter types define coercions.
+A box at the rule answers the draft note that asks what the intersection of two
+declarations is; the Meet Rule of \secref{overloading-static-params} gains the
+same case, with a box.
+The Meet Rule's example concludes that $V$ covers $S \inter T$, and that $f(V)$
+is applicable to and more specific for any call at run time to which $f(S)$ and
+$f(T)$ are applicable.
+\secref{principles-overloading} says that a static call whose argument's static
+type stands between a trait with a \KWD{comprises} clause and its listed types
+may have several declarations applicable to it that no other applicable
+declaration is more specific than, and is not a static error.
+The second of the two facts of \secref{overloading-coercion-resolution} keeps a
+single most specific declaration for the dynamic call and, but for such a call,
+for the static call; the declaration that the dynamic call runs is the same as
+or more specific than every declaration applicable to the static call, its
+return type a subtype of theirs; the type of a static call whose most specific
+declarations have no static parameters is the intersection of their return
+types; and a sentence gives the scope of the proof.
+In the internal document, the proposed feature on the intersection of two types
+with \KWD{comprises} clauses is marked done.
+\item[Rationale] This change does not follow from route~A; the revival decided
+on 29~September 2026 that the Meet Rule gains the case of declarations that
+together cover the intersection, and that a call whose argument's static type
+stands between two traits with \KWD{comprises} clauses is typed by the
+intersection of its candidates' return types, with the proof of
+\appref{overloaded-functional} revised to the uniqueness of the most specific
+declaration at run time (\secref{revival-proof}).
+The team's list of proposed features records the same plan for the example:
+``We agreed to revise the Meet rule to address this with the coverage check''.
+Under the reading of \secref{trait-decls}, the intersection of two traits with
+\KWD{comprises} clauses is not in general equal to a named type, and without the
+case the Meet Rule would refuse the example given to illustrate it.
+The case is an addition to the Meet Rule of the type group's paper of 2011,
+which asks for a declaration on the meet, as the type group's calculus
+Welterweight Fortress does (\nolinkurl{Papers/Welterweight/fig-meetrule.tick},
+in the revival's repository).
+The typing of such a call follows from the Return Type Rule: the declaration
+that runs is below every most specific declaration of the static call, and its
+return type below each of theirs.
+For a declaration with static parameters one instance would have to meet every
+one of those return types at once, which the proof does not show, so the typing
+is stated for declarations without static parameters only.
+The covering is a judgement of the overloading rules alone: it makes no type a
+subtype of another.
+The full reasoning is in
+\nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-spec-overloading/decision-record.md}
+and \nolinkurl{explorations/reviews/comprises-type-level-proof-addendum.md} in
+the revival's repository.
+\item[Effect] The Meet Rule's example is valid; both implementations refused it
+before this change (row~492 of the revival's gap ledger).
+A static call whose argument's static type stands between two traits with
+\KWD{comprises} clauses, as an instantiation of a trait with static parameters
+that extends both unlisted does, is not a static error: it runs the declaration
+that covers its value, and its type is the intersection of the return types of
+its most specific declarations.
+The Meet Rule for dotted methods keeps its form, asking for a declaration on the
+intersection (\secref{revival-notrevised}).
+\item[Original text] The Working Draft's rules are unchanged, the cases being
+added after them.
+\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/advanced/overloading.tex}, lines 303--307,
+the example's conclusion:
+\begin{quote}
+Because of the \KWD{comprises} clauses of $S$ and $T$ and the \KWD{excludes}
+clause of $U$, any subtype of both $S$ and $T$ must be a subtype of $V$.  Thus,
+$V = S \inter T$, and the declaration $f(V)$ ``disambiguates'' $f(S)$ and
+$f(T)$, i.e., it is applicable to and more specific for any call to which both
+$f(S)$ and $f(T)$ are applicable.
+\end{quote}
+and lines 460--468, the second fact and the sentence after the two:
+\begin{quote}
+If any declaration is applicable to a static call then there exists a single
+most specific declaration that is applicable to the static call and a single
+most specific declaration that is applicable to the corresponding dynamic call.
+
+Moreover, we can prove that the most specific declaration that is applicable to
+a dynamic call is more specific than the most specific declaration that is
+applicable to the corresponding static call.
+\end{quote}
+\item[Route C] The same under route~C.
+\end{description}
+
+\subsection{The proof of overloading resolution}
+\seclabel{revival-proof}
+
+\begin{description}
+\item[Affected section] \secref{proof-overloading-resolution}.
+\item[Change] The proof states its scope and its assumptions: declarations
+whose parameter and return types have no static parameters, calls to which
+declarations are applicable without coercion, the overloading rules, bodies
+that exist and are well typed, a sound and transitive subtype relation, and
+every value of a trait with a \KWD{comprises} clause a value of one of its
+listed types, which the compiled type checker does not yet enforce across
+components.
+It states the Meet Rule as it uses it: declarations below both parameter types
+that together hold every value of both, of which a declaration on the
+intersection is the case of one.
+Lemma~\ref{lem:le} proves only that the dynamic call has at most one most
+specific declaration, taking a covering declaration where it took the
+declaration on the intersection;
+Theorem~\ref{thm:overloading-subtyping} proves only that the dynamic call has
+exactly one when the static call has any;
+Theorem~\ref{thm:dynamic-subtype-static} proves that the declaration that runs
+is the same as or more specific than every declaration applicable to the static
+call; and a new Theorem~\ref{thm:result-type} proves that its return type is a
+subtype of the return type of every most specific declaration of the static
+call.
+The lemmas of existence are unchanged.
+\item[Rationale] This change does not follow from route~A; the revival decided
+on 29~September 2026, with the case of the Meet Rule of \secref{revival-meet},
+that the proof keeps its lemmas of existence and gives up the uniqueness of the
+most specific declaration for the static call for its uniqueness for the
+dynamic call, with its scope and its assumption on \KWD{comprises} clauses
+marked.
+Covering gives a declaration that holds the value of the argument, not one
+whose parameter type is a supertype of the static type of the argument, so the
+static call may have more than one most specific declaration.
+The type group's paper of 2019 keeps a unique most specific declaration for
+every call as a theorem (Park, Hong, Steele and Ryu, POPL 2019, Theorem~4.1);
+a call whose argument's static type stands between two traits with
+\KWD{comprises} clauses is outside that paper, which has no closed types, and
+the revival gives up the unique most specific declaration for the static call
+there on the assumptions this proof states.
+The full reasoning is in
+\nolinkurl{explorations/reviews/comprises-type-level-proof-addendum.md} and
+\nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-spec-overloading/decision-record.md}
+in the revival's repository.
+\item[Effect] The appendix proves that no call is undefined or ambiguous at run
+time within its scope and on its assumptions; it does not prove the soundness of
+declarations with static parameters, of inference or of coercion.
+Where a type declared in a later component escapes the check of a
+\KWD{comprises} clause (row~487 of the revival's gap ledger), the uniqueness of
+the most specific declaration for the dynamic call is not guaranteed.
+\item[Original text] \nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/appendices/overloading-function.tex},
+lines 37--48:
+\begin{quote}
+Below we prove: $|\Sigma| \neq 0$ implies $|\sigma| = 1$, and $|\Sigma| \neq 0$
+implies $|\delta| = 1$.
+Informally, if any declaration is applicable to a static call then there exists
+a single most specific declaration that is applicable to the static call and a
+single most specific declaration that is applicable to the corresponding
+dynamic call.
+\end{quote}
+lines 84--135, the lemma and the two theorems this change revises:
+\begin{quote}
+\emph{Lemma.} $|\sigma| \le 1$.  Also, $|\delta| \le 1$.
+
+\emph{Proof.} We prove this for $\delta$, but the case for $\sigma$ is
+identical.
+For the purpose of contradiction suppose there are two declarations
+$\f(\Ps)$ and $\f(\Qs)$ in $\delta$.  Since both $\f(\Ps)$ and
+$\f(\Qs)$ are applicable without coercion to the call $\f(\Xs)$ we
+have $\Xs \Ovrsubtype \Ps \inter \Qs$.  Therefore it is not the case
+that $\Ps \incompatible \Qs$.  By the overloading rules, $\Ps
+\neq \Qs$ and either $\Ps \excludes \Qs$ or there is a declaration
+$\f(\Ps \inter \Qs)$ visible at $Z$.  Since it cannot be the case that
+$\Ps \excludes \Qs$ there must exist a declaration $\f(\Ps \inter
+\Qs)$ visible at $Z$.  Since $\Ps \inter \Qs \Ovrsubtype \Ps$ and $\Ps
+\inter \Qs \Ovrsubtype \Qs$ we know $\f(\Ps \inter \Qs)$ is applicable
+without coercion to the call $\f(\Xs)$.  Since $\Ps \neq \Qs$ either
+$\Ps \inter \Qs \strictsubtype \Ps$ or $\Ps \inter \Qs \strictsubtype
+\Qs$.  Either case contradicts our assumption.
+
+\emph{Theorem.} If $|\Sigma| \neq 0$ then $|\sigma| = 1$.  Also, if
+$|\Sigma| \neq 0$ then $|\delta| = 1$.
+
+\emph{Proof.} Follows from the three lemmas before it.
+
+\emph{Theorem.} If $\sigma = \set{S}$ and $\delta = \set{D}$ then
+$D \Ovrsubtype S$.
+
+\emph{Proof.} If the declaration with parameter type $S$ and the declaration
+with parameter type $D$ satisfy the Subtype Rule then the theorem is
+proved.  Otherwise, by the definition of $\sigma$ we have $\sigma
+\subseteq \Sigma$.  Therefore $S \in \Sigma$.  By the first lemma,
+$S \in \Delta$.  Notice that $S,D \in \Delta$ implies
+$X \Ovrsubtype S$ and $X \Ovrsubtype D$.  Therefore, $S \not \excludes
+D$.  By the More Specific Rule for Functions, there must exist a
+declaration with parameter type $S \inter D$.  Because $X
+\Ovrsubtype (S \inter D)$, $(S \inter D) \in \Delta$.
+Notice $(S \inter D) \Ovrsubtype S$ and $(S \inter D) \Ovrsubtype D$.
+By the definition of $\delta$, we have $\lnot \exists D'\in\Delta: D'
+\strictsubtype D$.  In particular, $(S \inter D) \not \strictsubtype
+D$.  Therefore $(S \inter D) = D$.
+\end{quote}

## 2. The sentence and its history

- **The sentence.** "Although there may be multiple declarations with the same functional name, it is an error for their static parameters to differ (up to α-equivalence), or for one declaration to have static parameters and another to not have them. Hence, static parameters do not enter into the determination of which declarations are applicable, so we ignore them for most of this chapter" (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/overloading.tex:100-108`), with its echo "Overloaded declarations must have static parameters that are identical (up to α-equivalence) ... static parameters ... are ignore
- **Its date and author.** It is in the earliest reachable git copy of the LaTeX, `0f49d8698` (2009-11-06, Sukyoung Ryu, "[spec] Added the entire spec files. The next task is to integrate the technical decisions since 1.0.", `git show 0f49d8698:Specification/basic/overloading.tex`, line 108); the conversion severed the links before it (`research/authorship.md`), so its authoring commit is not recoverable (`explorations/reviews/mie-probes/spec-sentences-dated.md`).
- **The 1.0 section it displaced.** The Fortress 1.0 release of 2008 has instead Section 15.6.1, "Type Relationships with Static Parameters": "For type parameters, we use their bounds as their supertypes. As with the rest of this chapter, the type relations described in this section may be replaced when the static type checker and the type inference engine are implemented." (`Specification-1.0-frozen/fortress.1.0.pdf`, Section 15.6.1; read with `pdftotext`, the text at lines 5232-5238 of its output.) The section expected its own replacement.
- **Walk since 2007.** `3e05c3424` (2007-05-21, David Chase): "Changed overloading to implement (roughly) the "nice" proposal where functions with different numbers of static parameters can all be overloaded together"; `b176e1440` (2007-06-27, Jan-Willem Maessen): "Removed a tonne of gratuitous type parameters now that we support non-homogenous parameterization of overloadings". Neither path has enforced the sentence since (FACTS, "The compiled checker does not enforce the specification's sentence that overloads may not differ in static parameters").
- **The paper.** Allen, Hilburn, Kilpatrick, Luchangco, Ryu, Chase and Steele, OOPSLA 2011 (`Papers/Types/`): a generic declaration is applicable when one of its instances is (`Papers/Types/setup.tick:393-397`); specificity by applicable sets, checked as subtyping of existential domains (`Papers/Types/rules.tick:84-116`); the three rules (`rules.tick:158-180`); existential reduction (`Papers/Types/exc-reduction.tick:1-60`): under the assumption that an intersection is not `Bottom`, the constraints are gathered and unified, and where the premises fail the existential is related to itself, not t
- **The restart.** The team's 2012 restart of the chapter goes from the operator note straight on where the sentence stood (`Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/overloading.tick:100-114`), and its Types chapter gives function types holding arrow and universal arrow types together (`types.tick:553-558`, `:794-801`) and drops from a quantified type a static parameter that appears in none of its types (`:764-767`).
- **The way back and its price.** Enforcing the sentence (the overloading judgement's option 3) refuses every set with differing lists on both paths, lifted methods included: 179 library api pairs under the narrow reading and 335 under the wide one, the tower's own method implementations among them (`explorations/reviews/mie-probes/scope-call-site-dispatch.md`; `explorations/reviews/overloading-judgement.md` section 3.2), and it would undo `b176e1440`'s removal of the padding. It is the route back if the model is ever abandoned; the Appendix I entry keeps the sentence's text.

- `Specification/basic/overloading.tex:100-110`: declarations of one name may differ in their static parameters; a declaration with static parameters is read over its instances. `:149-155`: the static arguments a call writes are substituted; those it does not write are inferred after the selection. `:194-199` and `:235-239`: applicability when some instance within the bounds is (named and dotted calls). `:365-375`: specificity by applicable sets, the paper's definition; "No static arguments are inferred for the comparison".

The inference chapter is cited, not restated.
- **The POPL recheck's item 1.4, a default.** The Appendix I entry "Overloading with static parameters" says in one sentence that the POPL 2019 paper's soundness proof excludes a type parameter named in another's upper bound (restriction 2, p. 11:11) and closed types (pp. 11:3, 11:25), so the library's `SUM`, `BIG MAX` and `Integral` families rest on the 2011 rules as the checker implements them, not on the 2019 proof.
- **The calculus.** Core Fortress with Overloading's rule [Valid] asks, for two declarations with the same number of parameters, that their static parameters' bounds be the same under renaming (`Specification/appendices/calculi/overloading/static.tex:172-192`, case 2(1)). It admits fewer overloadings than the revised chapters, so its valid programs stay valid Fortress programs; under POSITIONS 2026-09-26 (rung S's stop on the calculi, option 1) the calculi keep their rules and soundness claims, and the entry's Effect names it.

## 4. The implicit bound and the naked-`Any` rule (Q1, POSITIONS 2026-09-29, the implicit bound)

- `Specification/basic/trait-parameters.tex:49-62`: `extends Any`, with a callout: the Working Draft's `Object` (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/trait-parameters.tex:49-50`); `Any` holds tuples and `()`, which `Object` does not (`Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick:232-236`); the POPL 2019 paper's default (section 3.2, p. 11:9; the POPL recheck's item 1.7, a default); row 412, the compile path's `Object` setting (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/desugarer/PreDisambiguationDesugaringVisitor.java:74-86`), until the switch-over.
- The naked-`Any` rule, stated as the compiled checker applies it: a bound written `Any`. The checker's test is `checkBoundAny` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/OverloadingChecker.scala:430-439`, applied at `:375-378`), which looks for an `AnyType` in the parameter's `extends` clause. Measured on the base (section 10): a written `extends Any` is refused, "A functional which takes a single parameter of a parametric type bound by Any cannot be overloaded"; an unwritten bound is not. The library's value factory pair, `array1[\T, nat s0\]()` and `array1[\T, nat s0\](v:T)` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:1572-1573`), draws no such refusal: the last landed gate's per-site list, which runs the overloading check over the one library, has no line with that message and no `array1` line (`explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-6.5b/gate/distance-sites.tsv`, 625 lines; `git log e3214cbf1..811053f15 -- Library/ ProjectFortress/` prints nothing, so the table is the base's).
- The example `makeSet` and its explanation are kept (the overloading judgement, section 3.4: "The naked-`Any` rule stays"). Read under the model, the pair is also refused by the Return Type Rule over every instance (`makeSet`'s instance at `(ZZ, ZZ)` returns `Set[\(ZZ, ZZ)\]`, and no instance of the two-parameter declaration applicable to `(ZZ, ZZ)` returns a subtype of it); the text does not say so, no decision having asked for it. Reported, not written.
- The rationale of Appendix I's `tabulate` entry (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex`, `\secref{revival-tabulate}`) says "the implicit bound `Object` of \secref{type-param}". It is batch 7's record of 26 September's reasoning; item 23's decision has this rung change no other entry, so the implicit-bound entry's Effect says that the rationale predates the change. A decision (section 11, decision 5).

## 5. The dispatch sentence (item 30 and the paper's instance rule)

- `Specification/basic/overloading.tex:312-332` in the dispatch paragraph, the callout `:333-349`, the examples `:377-405` after the definition of "more specific".

== basic/overloading.tex:100-108
Although there may be multiple declarations
with the same functional name,
it is an error for their static parameters to differ
(up to $\alpha$-equivalence),
or for one declaration to have static parameters
and another to not have them.
Hence, static parameters do not enter into the determination of which
declarations are applicable,
so we ignore them for most of this chapter.
== basic/overloading.tex:137-138
We assume throughout this chapter that all static variables in functional calls
have been instantiated or inferred.
== basic/overloading.tex:173-175
If the parameter type $\Ps$ includes static parameters,
they are inferred as described in \chapref{type-inference}
before checking the applicability of the declaration to the call.
== basic/overloading.tex:205-207
If the types $\Ps_0$ and $\Ps$ include static parameters,
they are inferred as described in \chapref{type-inference}
before checking the applicability of the declaration to the call.
== basic/overloading.tex:292-295
If the declarations include static parameters,
they are inferred as described in \chapref{type-inference}
before comparing their parameter types
to determine which declaration is more specific.
== basic/overloading.tex:263-276
To evaluate a given functional call,
it is necessary to determine which functional declaration
to dispatch to.
To do so,
we consider the declarations that are applicable to that call at run time.
If there is exactly one such declaration,
then the call dispatches to that declaration.
If there is no such declaration,
then the call is \emph{undefined}, which is a static error.
(However, see \secref{applicability-with-coercion}
for how coercion may add to the set of applicable declarations.)
If multiple declarations are applicable to the call at run time,
then we choose an arbitrary declaration among the declarations such that
no other applicable declaration is more specific than them.
== advanced/overloading.tex:95-103
Overloaded declarations must have static parameters that are identical
(up to $\alpha$-equivalence).  Also, valid overloadings for
declarations that contain keyword or
varargs parameters are determined
by analyzing the expansion of these declarations as described in
\secref{applicability-with-special-params}.  Therefore, static
parameters, keyword parameters,
and varargs parameters are ignored in
the remainder of this chapter.

== advanced/overloading.tex:303-307
Because of the \KWD{comprises} clauses of $S$ and $T$ and the \KWD{excludes}
clause of $U$, any subtype of both $S$ and $T$ must be a subtype of
$V$.  Thus, $V = S \inter T$, and the declaration $f(V)$
``disambiguates'' $f(S)$ and $f(T)$, i.e., it is applicable to and more
specific for any call to which both $f(S)$ and $f(T)$ are applicable.
== advanced/overloading.tex:460-468
If any declaration is applicable to a static call then there exists a
single most specific declaration that is applicable to the static call
and a single most specific declaration that is applicable to the
corresponding dynamic call.
\end{enumerate}

Moreover, we can prove that the most specific declaration that is
applicable to a dynamic call is more specific than the most specific
declaration that is applicable to the corresponding static call.

If a type parameter does not have an \KWD{extends} clause, it has an
implicit ``\EXP{\KWD{extends} \TYP{Object}}'' clause.

content.content:
### 4.2 The dynamic choice (§5.2, pp. 11:16-21)

- **The contract.** "dynamic overloading resolution then must select an
  instance of the most specific method declaration that is applicable to the
  dynamic types of the arguments and whose return type is a subtype of the
  static type of the expression" (p. 11:15).
- **Types at run time.** Types are reified: "all the type parameters are
  instantiated with ground types at run time", and a value's run-time type is
  its *ilk* (p. 11:17). Ground types include unions and intersections
  (Fig. 8, p. 11:17).
- **[R-Method]** (p. 11:17). It sorts the visible declarations most-to-least
  specific ("This order is statically determinable, so the sorting can be
  done at compile time"). It then runs the *dispatch semipredicate* on each
  declaration in turn and takes the first that succeeds. The receiver's ilk is
  matched together with the arguments' ilks, which is what makes the dispatch
  symmetric.
- **The semipredicate** ([Dispatch], pp. 11:17-18) has three steps:
  1. match the argument ilks against the domain to get lower and upper bounds
     for the method type parameters;
  2. match the call's static return type against the declared return type to
     get bounds "to make sure that the dynamic dispatch preserves type";
  3. solve the bounds.

  "If any of these steps fails, the semipredicate is false: the declaration
  is not applicable" (p. 11:18). Matching a union can yield several candidate
  bound lists, combined as a Cartesian product (pp. 11:18-19).
- **Solving** (Fig. 10, p. 11:19). The rule works from the rightmost type
  parameter to the left and "computes a substitution … by taking the
  intersection of the upper bounds", declared and computed. It then
  propagates the choice into the declared lower bounds of the parameters to
  its left. It "never instantiates method type parameters with Bottom". The
  right-to-left pass works because of the binding restrictions (p. 11:11):
  - a method type parameter's scope "extends to the right of its
    declaration";
  - "no reference to a method type parameter appears in any of the upper
    bounds";
  - the union of the lower bounds must be below the intersection of the upper
    bounds.
- **The worked example** (§5.2.4, pp. 11:20-21).
  - Two covariant `append` declarations, over `SortedList` and over `List`.
  - The call has static type `List⟦C3⟧` and argument ilks `SortedCons⟦C1⟧`
    and `Cons⟦C2⟧`, with C1, C2 <: C3.
  - The `SortedList` declaration fails on the second argument, so the `List`
    one runs, instantiated at `[C3/P, C3/Q]`.
  - So the instance comes from the static return type's upper bound, not from
    the ilks' C1 and C2.
- **Why intersection of upper bounds.** The Fortress team "had assumed …
  that once the tightest possible upper and lower bounds for a method type
  parameter have been found, then the union (or pseudo-union) of the lower
  bounds should be chosen". For that and for a hybrid "we were unable to
  complete the proofs of correctness", so the algorithm "always chooses the
  intersection of the upper bounds" (p. 11:25).
- **Union instances.** A type parameter can be instantiated at a union at
  run time. In the paper's example `O.m(3, true): (Int ⊔ Boolean)`, "P of m
  is inferred as (Int ⊔ Boolean) by the dispatch semipredicate at run time"
  (p. 11:21).

## 5. The run-time check on the return type

- **What it is.** Every call carries its static return type into run time
  (§5.1, p. 11:16). Dispatch uses it as an upper bound when it instantiates
  the chosen declaration (p. 11:18).
- **It never moves a call to another declaration.**
  - Lemma 5.8: whatever instance the checker chose, "there exists a
    type-safe most specific method instance at run time" (p. 11:22). Its proof
    is where [Return-Test] is used (pp. 11:22-23).
  - Lemma 5.9: the first-dispatchable scan then yields an instance of the
    most specific declaration applicable to the ilks, with a return type below
    the static one (p. 11:23).
  - In a well-formed program the return-type bounds therefore never rule out
    that declaration. They only choose its instance.
- **What it costs.**
  - "In simple invariant cases, we expect the run-time cost to be relatively
    low but nonzero", since matching `List⟦String⟧` against `List⟦T⟧` only
    binds T (pp. 11:24-25).
  - For the covariant and contravariant cases, "caching or dynamic
    recompilation … may help" (p. 11:25).
  - The discussion calls left-to-right scoping "a relatively small sacrifice
    of expressivity for a large gain in dynamic efficiency" (p. 11:24).

## 6. What it proves and what it leaves open

### C. The return-type rule and the positional rule, `rung-return-type-rule`

**The answers this rung follows.** Q4 = (1), answer 9's rule; item 26 = (1), decided by Pavol on 2026-09-29 with the three points of Astra's proof addendum built into this batch's briefs (POSITIONS 2026-09-29, PLAN item 26); item 30 = (1), decided by Pavol on 2026-09-29, its judgement's option 1 
(POSITIONS 2026-09-29, PLAN item 30), at the instance the paper's rule gives; the paper's instance rule, decided by Pavol on 2026-09-29 (POSITIONS 2026-09-29, a type parameter that a call's arguments do not fix); the POPL recheck's item 1.4, the recommended default while Pavol has not answered. 
(Section 1 of the record gives each question and its options. Text marked "under Q4 = (2)", "under item 26 = (1)" or "under item 30 = (1)" applies only while the coordinator has written that answer here.)

**The problem.** Two defects of the compiled checker's overloading rules, both measured.
- The return-type rule solves the match of two declarations' domains once and checks that one instance (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/overloading/OverloadingOracle.scala`, `satisfiesReturnTypeRule`, `:81-117`), where the paper requires it of every applicable instance 
(`Papers/Types/rules.tick:174-180`; the theorem at `Papers/Types/overloading-check.tick:166-172`). So the paper's own counterexample, a generic declaration returning its type parameter beside a plain declaration on a subtype returning that subtype, type-checks, and the JVM verifier then refuses the 
class, "Bad return type"; walk refuses the pair when it loads (`explorations/reviews/overload-static-params-ways.md` section 2.2, probe `GenPlainRTR`, and section 2.3, defect 2).
- An override whose return type reorders its own static parameters type-checks, and the compiled run dies with `ClassCastException`, because a call that writes its static arguments hands them by position to whichever declaration dispatch reaches (row 398; FACTS.md, "The checker's return-type rule 
lets the more specific declaration choose its own instantiation"; probes `SubOvSwapTRun`, `explorations/compile-ladder/rung-nat-checker/probes/compile-probes.txt:29-33`, and `PermuteReturn`); walk refuses the binding. The specification refuses the pair 
(`Specification/advanced/overloading.tex:95-103`, `:158-170`), and the paper accepts it, because it has no written static arguments (`explorations/reviews/overloading-judgement.md` section 8, first item).
Beside them:
- Row 492: the checker refuses the specification's own Meet Rule example, `f(S)`, `f(T)` and `f(V)` over `S comprises {U, V}` and `T comprises {V, W}`, "Invalid overloading of f", at `validOverloading` in `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/OverloadingChecker.scala` 
(`:418`), because nothing reads the meet of two closed traits from their clauses. It is gated as the expected failure `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/XXXComprisesMeetCompiled.test`. Walk's half is rung W's (PLAN.md, phase 3, batch 7b's line; `explorations/reviews/batch-7C-review.md`, finding 2).
- Row 499: since batch 6.5's rung G the compiled dispatcher tests a generic declaration at the call's type arguments, by position (FACTS.md, "A generic arm of a template dispatcher is called at the dispatcher's own static parameters"), and two programs the checker accepts, `SkPosBox` and 
`SkPosFixed`, now answer with the less specific declaration (`explorations/compile-ladder/rung-generic-runtime/probes/skeptic/dispatch-pos.txt`). Both declarations of each pair return `String` (`SkPosBox.fss:7-8`, `SkPosFixed.fss:11-12`), so the positional rule as answer 9 words it accepts them, 
and only the domain condition refuses them (section 1, Q4). Under item 30 = (1) the specification gives the more specific declaration, whose parameter the value fixes at an invariant position (`Box[\U\]`, `Fixed[\Y\]`), so that the paper's instance rule and the value's type agree, and under Q4 = 
(1) the two programs' compiled answers contradict the text: a defect of the template dispatcher, gated here and repaired in phase 5.
- Not this rung's repair, and its expected failures this rung's: code generation fails for two generic declarations on a bare type variable, with a duplicate class name or unreadable serialized data (defect 3; probes `GenBoundedFix`, `GenBoundedFixU`); a dispatcher that is not a template, a generic 
declaration beside a plain one, dies on rung G's two programs, on a `ZZ32` spelled two ways (row 494's remainder) and on a cast to the arm's return type spelled with its own parameter (row 496; `explorations/reviews/plain-beside-generic-judgement.md` section 6). A generic dotted method keeps rung 
G's dispatch defects too (row 495, gated since rung G).
- Under the paper's instance rule (POSITIONS 2026-09-29, a type parameter that a call's arguments do not fix; `explorations/reviews/decisions-review/popl-recheck.md` sections 1.2, 1.6 and 1.9), three pieces of evidence the text will now call for, none of them a repair of this rung's. First, the 
instance of a generic declaration reached only at run time whose type parameter the value does not fix: the text gives the parameter's declared bound under what the call's static type requires of the return type, and the compiled path takes the value's type, since its code generator reads a 
dispatched arm's static arguments from the value's descriptor (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/OverloadSet.java:1484`, "Runtime inference for some cases") and does not pass the call's static return type (`:2048`, "Not sure what to do with return type"); where the value fixes the 
parameter the two agree, as in every program of rows 496 and 499. The recheck's shape (its section 1.6): a generic declaration returning `Box[\T\]`, with `T` the whole type of one of its parameters, reached only at run time from a call that the static types sent to a plain declaration returning 
`Any`, whose argument holds a `ZZ32`: the text gives `Box[\Any\]`, the value's type `Box[\ZZ32\]`. The specification refuses `id[\T\](x: T)` beside `id(x: Any)` under the bound `Any`, by the naked-`Any` rule (`Specification/advanced/overloading.tex:114-127`) and by No Duplicates, so the generic 
declaration takes a second parameter that the static call cannot match and the value can, or a written bound (with `X extends Number` the text gives `Box[\Number\]`); the shape is the rung's. Second, the paper's own valid overload set that domain subtyping alone cannot show valid (POPL 2019, p. 
11:13): `m[\P\](x: ArrayList[\P\])`, `m[\Q extends T\](y: List[\Q\])` and `m[\R extends T\](z: ArrayList[\R\])`, `ArrayList` extending `List`, both invariant, which the paper accepts through its existential reduction (p. 11:14) and the revival's checker, whose reduction forces equalities through 
instantiation exclusion only, may refuse (the recheck's section 1.2). Third, the compiled test of a lone type parameter, `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/XXXInferLoneBoundUnion`, which asserts that `pick0(w, r)` and the bounded `pick(w, r)` are both instances at the union (row 516): the text now

coercion attempt's candidates, `Functionals.scala:334-343`, by reading).

**The decisions.** Answer 9 (`explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md`, 2026-09-26, answer 9): the checker keeps the paper's three rules with two changes, the return-type rule checked over every instance, and two generic declarations in the more-specific relation agreeing on their static parameters 
position by position, which closes row 398. The recommendation's description is `explorations/reviews/overloading-judgement.md` section 3.5; its account of one way to build the first change (the less specific declaration's parameters kept quantified except where the domains force an equality, as 
rung N already keeps a size) is one way among those the rung lists, not the brief, and probe P1 measured that way working (below). The positional rule's condition is Q4's answer: under Q4 = (1) the return type's alone, as the judgement words it; under Q4 = (2) the parameter types too, Java's 
condition for overriding. Not the checker step of the judgement's option 2 (an exclusion concluded from a bound), which answer 9 declined. Defect 3 gets a ledger row and an expected-failure compiler test, and its fix stays on phase 5's code-generation list (judgement section 3.7; the conversion 
judgement's sections 5 and 7, which leave it there with no new reach). Row 492's checker half and the typing of a call that sits between two closed traits, under item 26 = (1): the five paragraphs after this one. Under item 30 = (1) (its judgement's section 6): row 496's two crashes get 
expected-failure compiled tests here, their repair staying on phase 5's code-generation list; and the checker's dynamic-applicability annotation, `isDynamicallyApplicable` in `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/useful/STypesUtil.scala`, which reads the other answer and which nothing 
reads, is left as it is and named in the report and in a note on row 496. Under the paper's instance rule (POSITIONS 2026-09-29, a type parameter that a call's arguments do not fix): the first piece of evidence above gets one expected-failure pair in the two-file form, its repair on phase 5's list, 
where the compiled dispatcher receives the call's static return type; the second gets a test, plain if the checker accepts the set and an expected failure pinned by its refusal if it refuses it, the refusal a ledger row this rung opens (the recheck's section 1.2), and no checker change, since the 
paper's existential reduction is a reduction beyond the one answer 9 took, and a rule beyond the paper's three and the positional rule is a stop; the third is turned into a plain test of the written bound, and the unbounded case gets its own expected failure, since the text now settles it and the 
rule of 2026-09-19 gives a deferred defect the text settles an `XXX` test (POSITIONS 2026-09-19, the six process decisions), for batch 8's checker rung to flip. Under the POPL recheck's item 1.4, a default: the decision record says in one sentence that the paper's soundness proof excludes a type 
parameter named in another's upper bound (restriction 2, p. 11:11) and closed types (p. 11:3, p. 11:25), so the library's `SUM`, `BIG MAX` and `Integral` families, and item 26's coverage case, rest on the 2011 rules as this checker implements them and on the proof addendum, not on the 2019 proof.

**Row 492's checker half, under item 26 = (1).** It is this rung's by PLAN.md's routing and a requirement of Pavol's decision, so that rung S's closed-trait case of the Meet Rule states a rule the checker runs (`explorations/reviews/comprises-type-level-judgement.md` section 6; the proof addendum's 
review of this brief, `explorations/reviews/comprises-type-level-proof-addendum.md`, "Application to the existing brief" and "Review of the 7b briefing, at the same base"). What the checker must establish before it accepts two overlapping declarations whose domains are neither below the other, in 
plain words (the addendum's Cover-Meet): visible concrete declarations whose domains are each strictly below both domains, and so applicable to every value they hold, together hold every value of the overlap, every value a program could make and not only the values a test makes; the same holds for 
every such pair of the family, the covering declarations' own pairs among them; an overlap that is empty, because the two domains exclude, needs no covering declaration. The judgement's device can serve it: in the meet search of `validOverloading`, an intersection whose conjuncts have `comprises` 
clauses is expanded by them, a pair that excludes dropped, and the result compared with the declared domains, so that the intersection of `S comprises {U, V}` and `T comprises {V, W}`, with `U excludes W`, is covered by `V`. The expansion is a finite argument from the declared clauses, not a list 
of observed objects: it substitutes a trait's static arguments into its clause correctly, proves each covering domain below both competitors, drops only the exclusions it proves, and covers the whole remaining overlap; a case it cannot settle is a refusal, never an acceptance. Its recursion is 
bounded by cycle detection, not by an assumed depth of the clauses, and the rung watches for the stack overflow Steele met in the subtyping version (the lines he commented out in `TypeAnalyzer.scala`, `59fdeff62`). The device is the rung's, listed among the ways.

**The coverage check stays local to overload checking.** It answers whether an overload family is valid, and justifies the typing of a call that sits between two closed traits (below), and nothing else: a coverage result never becomes an ordinary subtyping or assignment fact. The normalizer's 
existing rule is the expansion's one-clause case: `normConjunct` in `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/types/TypeAnalyzer.scala` (`:645-655` on `3ec367f4d`) shrinks a closed conjunct by its clause when another conjunct excludes one of its listed types, which the judgement measured 
working on the compiled path (`MeetViaExclusion`, compiled `PASS`; its control `MeetViaExclusionNoV`, refused; `explorations/reviews/comprises-type-level-judgement/probes/`). That normalizer is shared: `subtype`, `meet` and `equivalent` normalize through it (`:85-86`, `:78-79`, `:314-315`), so on 
`MeetViaExclusion`'s shape ordinary subtyping already reaches `V`, and the checker's line between coverage and subtyping is already mixed (the addendum, "The normalizer boundary is already mixed"). The rung reuses the clause and exclusion helpers as it needs, and does not broaden the shared 
normalizer, `subtype`, `meet` or `equivalent`: every general subtype, assignment and equivalence verdict stays as it is in this rung, and repairing the normalizer's own consistency is separate work. `SkBetweenAssign`'s refusal alone cannot show that no such verdict moved, since a change can reach 
an explicitly written intersection or union that program does not use; so the rung's diff leaves those functions, and their callers outside the overloading check, as they are, and a change there is the fallback's condition (below), its assignment and equivalence consequences reported, not made.

**The call that sits between two closed traits, and coercion.** A call whose argument's static type sits between two closed traits (`BetweenTwoClosed`'s `g: G[\ZZ32\]`, `explorations/compile-ladder/rung-spec-comprises/probes/between/BetweenTwoClosed.fss`; and the ways note's `OwnClauseBetween`, 
`explorations/reviews/comprises-type-level-ways.md`, "For batch 7b's record") has several minimal unconverted candidates, where the checker today takes the first of a sort. Rung I's ambiguity check (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/impls/Functionals.scala`, `:688-752` on

input.description: Read the overloading judgement's options

content.content:
- The checker does not enforce the sentence. It checks every pair by the paper's rules and refuses only pairs it cannot prove unambiguous: `SCMP`/`PCMP`, overloaded over one, two and three static parameters, draw no error because their domains (a scalar, a pair, a triple) exclude structurally (`RangeInternals.fsi:30-40`; probe `DifferExcl`). What fails is open traits nothing declares exclusive, and one reasoning step (`CAP`, below). Source: `reviews/overload-static-params-ways.md` §§ 2, 5.
- Forced past the api's early return, the overloading check reports 482 errors, of which 175 (132 generic-plus-plain return-type errors and 43 duplicates) have a plain arm on a tower or `Comparison` type that the checker reports as excluding its own supertypes: the nested tower's, which route A flattens. That attribution is by reading; the worker did not re-run on a flat library, and the count of what survives is the first measurement the phase-3 batch takes (§ 3.8). The families that are this judgement's: `CAP` 17, `MIN`/`MAX` 8 plus 2, `openRangeHelper` 3, `seq` 5, juxtaposition 3, `CMP` 2 and `MINMAX` 2 (tower-shaped).
- walk's rule is the instantiation reading with a load-time check: each generic arm is instantiated from the arguments and the first strictly more specific instance is kept (`OverloadedFunction.java:856-895`), after a check that arms with generic parameters have "at least one pair of parameters [with] excluding types" unless a self parameter or an object type settles it (`:416-425`, `:519-527`). So walk accepts `GenPlainSub` and prints `generic` three times where the compiled path prints `circle, generic, circle`, and prints `circle, generic, circle` itself when the plain arm is declared first (capture `GenPlainSub.txt`): declaration order decides. That is defect 1.
- The checker's return-type rule solves the domain match once and checks that one instance (`OverloadingOracle.scala:81-117`), where the paper asks for every instance (`rules.tick:174-180`, the theorem at `overloading-check.tick:166-172`). So the paper's own counterexample, `ident[\T <: Shape\](x: T): T` beside `ident(x: Round): Round`, passes the checker and the JVM verifier refuses the class ("Bad return type", capture `GenPlainRTR.txt`); walk refuses the pair at load. That is defect 2.
- The sentence's dates: 2009 text (Sukyoung Ryu, `0f49d8698`), untouched since (`reviews/mie-probes/spec-sentences-dated.md`); the 1.0 release of March 2008 has instead §15.6.1, bounds as supertypes, "may be replaced when the static type checker and the type inference engine are implemented" (`Specification-1.0-frozen/fortress.1.0.pdf`); walk's relaxation is `3e05c3424` (2007-05-21, Chase, "the 'nice' proposal where functions with different numbers of static parameters can all be overloaded together"); the padding's removal `b176e1440` (2007-06-27, Maessen); the checker's rule `a7f149194` (2009-10, Kilpatrick, uninferable arms not dispatched); the paper 2011; the restart's overloading chapter (`overloading.tick:100-114`) goes from the operator note straight on where the sentence stood, and keeps only "inferred ... before comparing" (`:299-302`).
- The team's own doubt is in the specification: "Relaxing restrictions on static parameters of overloaded functionals", with Jan's `array1` pair and Marc's `conjugate` pair, and "What is the exclusion rule for a pair of overloaded declarations with different static parameters?" (`appendices/future.tex:236-266`).

### 3.2 The options, the library's own way first

1. **The library's practice made the rule.** Overloads across different lists, checkable by declared exclusion or avoided by names; the specification revised to the paper's model; the families repaired by the library's devices (the clean list's options 1 and 3). Commits him to: a specification rung; a checker rung (defect 2, the positional rule of § 3.5); a walk rung (defect 1); a library rung (§ 3.6). Cost: four rungs in one phase-3 batch, disjoint files. Reversal: the sentence's text is preserved in the appendix entry; enforcing it later is option 3's cost.
2. **The same, with the checker taught the missing reasoning step** for `CAP` and the object witness (the clean list's option 4, its way 11): conclude that two domains exclude when the only way they could meet contradicts a bound. Commits him to an extension beyond the paper, a soundness argument to write, and a specification paragraph the paper does not have; saves a handful of plain traits.
3. **Enforce the sentence** (the clean list's option 2). Commits him to both paths refusing every set with differing lists, lifted methods included, so every numeric operator against its algebraic trait; renaming or padding across the library, undoing `b176e1440`; 179 library api pairs refused under the narrow reading and 335 under the wide one, the tower's own method implementations among them (`reviews/mie-probes/scope-call-site-dispatch.md`, FACTS 2026-09-23); the padding clashes with the checker's rule that an arm whose parameters cannot be inferred is never dispatched. Against the library's practice and the type group's later word.
4. **Make walk the standard** (the clean list's option 6): drop the refusals walk does not make. Gives up the static guarantee the JVM verifier already enforces (`GenPlainRTR` is exactly what walk cannot catch and the verifier does). Against microGPT compiled.
5. **A rule that every static parameter must be fixed by the parameter types or a witness** (the clean list's option 5). Taken in its call-site form as question 3; its declaration form would refuse the library's own factories (`array1[\T, nat s0\]()` has both parameters in the return type only) and reopen E2.

### 3.3 The decision and why

Option 1. Derived from the fixed ground:
- *The library's practice is the standard* (POSITIONS 2026-09-19). The practice is overloading across lists since 2007, with 45 numbered declarations where names were easier, plain exclusion traits where a where-clause `excludes` cannot be written, and the `typecase`-on-thrower factory where two bounds would have made two arms. Option 1 is that practice; options 3 and 5 refuse it.
- *The type group's late, implementation-informed positions outweigh early specification text* (POSITIONS 2026-09-23). The sentence is the early text (2009); the paper (2011), the checker (2009-2012), Welterweight (2012) and the restart's Types chapter (2012, universal arrow types and function types holding generic and plain arms together, `types.tick:553-558`, `:794-801`) are the late positions, and they say option 1. The restart dropped the sentence.
- *No open discrepancy between the specification and the implementation* (POSITIONS 2026-09-24). Today the sentence describes neither path. Option 1 makes the text say what the checker does, with the original preserved and the way back priced.
- *microGPT compiled and fast* (2026-09-16). Option 1 costs no run-time mechanism; option 2 costs checker work with no library need once the plain traits exist; option 3 would rewrite the tower's operators on the way to the flattening.

This agrees with the S2 judgement: the rule S states (instantiation exclusion) is what makes the paper's reasoning about `CAP` and the `baz` repair possible at all, and the revised overloading chapter cites it rather than restating it.

content.content:
11. **Exclusion derived from MIE.** Two instantiations of one trait exclude unless their
    arguments are equal (`types.tick:355-360`, `introduction.tick:420-426`); the paper
    derives it inside existential types by "existential reduction"
    (`Papers/Types/exc-reduction.tick`). The checker does this for ground arguments
    (`MIEGround` passes) but cannot conclude exclusion when the only way two domains could
    meet contradicts a bound (`DifferMIE`: `S[\I extends Num[\I\]\] <: R[\I\]` against
    `P[\I,J\] <: R[\(I,J)\]`, where `I` would have to be a tuple). Neither the paper's rule
    ("otherwise" relates the type to itself) nor the code (`TypeSchemaAnalyzer.scala:215-221`,
    the unreduced meet is kept) draws that conclusion. Drawing it is sound, but it is an
    extension, not the paper.
12. **Run-time instantiation restricted by the return type** (Karl Naden, 2012,
    `Papers/RuntimeInstantiation/2012-6-15 ...txt:1-20`, `RTRinstantionTheory.tex`): when
    dispatch picks a more specific generic arm, its static parameters are bound so that its
    return type fits the one the checker used, including a parameter that appears only in
    the return type (`f[\P\](x: String): empty[\P\]`, same file). Not implemented.

(* The CAP family's shape (RangeInternals.fsi:44-99): S[\I\] extends R[\I\],
   P[\I,J\] extends R[\(I,J)\].  A type extending both would extend R[\I\] and
   R[\(I',J')\]; multiple instantiation exclusion then needs I = (I',J'), which
   the bound I extends Num[\I\] (a trait) rules out, since trait types exclude
   tuple types.  So the two arms exclude, by that chain of reasoning only. *)
component DifferMIE
export Executable
trait R[\T extends Any\] end
trait Num[\I extends Num[\I\]\] end
object Z extends Num[\Z\] end
trait S[\I extends Num[\I\]\] extends R[\I\] end
trait P[\I extends Num[\I\], J extends Num[\J\]\] extends R[\(I, J)\] end
object Sz extends S[\Z\] end
object Pz extends P[\Z, Z\] end
kind[\I extends Num[\I\]\](a: S[\I\]): String = "scalar"
kind[\I extends Num[\I\], J extends Num[\J\]\](a: P[\I, J\]): String = "pair"
run(): () = do
  println(kind(Sz))
  println(kind(Pz))
end
end

input.description: Read the paper's existential reduction

content.content:
In the evaluation of valid overloadings from Section~\ref{sec:examples},
intensional type analysis was required in order to reason about certain
examples. Since this reasoning justified
the validity of these overloaded functions, we incorporate it into
the present formal system as well.

Whenever two different domain types should be
applicable to the same argument type $W$ (in order to validate the Meet Rule
or Return Type Rule), an existentially quantified intersection type
naturally arises as the necessary supertype of $W$.
Intersection types $S \cap T$ in our type system naturally fall into two
distinct cases: either $S \nexc T$, or $S \exc T$ in which case the 
intersection has the same extent as \Bottom.
In the second case, the intersection is trivial and $W$, as
a subtype of the intersection, must also be trivial.
Moreover, because the argument type $W$ to which both declarations must be applicable
is necessarily equivalent to \Bottom, then the Meet Rule and Return Type Rule
are both trivially satisfied by the presence of the implicit overloading on
\Bottom. In this manner case analysis on whether an existentially
quantified (intersection) type is \Bottom facilitates the checking of our
rules.

Na\"{i}vely one might expect this case analysis on $S \cap T$ to simply check
whether $S \exc T$. However, as is the case when checking generic
function declarations, the types $S$ and $T$ might have free type variables,
whose uncertainty often precludes a definitive statement about $S \exc T$.
(For example, `C[\X\]` $\exc$ `C[\Y\]` holds only if $X \not\equiv Y$.) Our solution is to reason backwards: Under the assumption that the intersection
is nontrivial (that the types do not exclude), gather the necessary
constraints on type parameters. (For example, `C[\X\] CAP C[\Y\]` $\not\equiv \Bottom$ yields the constraint $X \equiv Y$.) These constraints are then
reduced, resulting in an instantiation (and potentially tighter bounds
on type parameters) that necessarily follows from our assumption of nontriviality.%
\footnote{A similar sort of case analysis and constraint solving
arises for pattern matching with generalized algebraic data types (GADTs) \cite{simonet07}: GADTs resemble our existential types and pattern matching resembles our function application.}


We call the general pattern of simplifying an existentially quantified
(intersection) type \emph{existential reduction}, given by the judgment $\jtred{\delta}{\delta}$ in Figure~\ref{fig:exred}. The first rule for existential reduction performs the constraint-based case analysis described above, while the second merely relates the existential to itself if the premises of the first rule do not hold. We thus explain the first rule in more detail.

The first premise determines the constraints $\C$ that must be true under
the hypothesis that $T \not\equiv \Bottom$ (i.e. that this type is
nontrivial). Note that the type variables from $\Delta$ are bound, while any
type variables from the existential itself, $\Delta'$, become inference type
variables mentioned in $\C$. The second premise binds $\C'$ to exactly
the inference type variables and bounds denoted by the existential's type parameters; these are the constraints that must hold for $T$ to still make
sense.
In the third premise, if \textit{unify} succeeds, it
produces a substitution $\phi$ for any inference type variables from $\Delta'$ constrained by equalities. Because $\phi$ is a most general unifier, it has the property that any other valid substitution $\psi$ of $\Delta'$'s variables with
$\psi(T) \not\equiv \Bottom$ must be equal to $\tau \circ \phi$, for some
other substitution $\tau$. Moreover, if \textit{unify} succeeds, it produces
a set of leftover constraints $\C''$ that are not unifiable equalities (but have still
been simplified).
If it is possible to express $\C''$ as some type environment $\Delta''$,
then we use this as the new type parameters over the simplified type
$\phi(T)$.

Similarly we call the general pattern of simplifying a universally quantified arrow type \emph{universal reduction}, given by the judgment $\jtred{\sigma_1}{\sigma_2}$
The first premise reduces the domain type $\dom(\sigma) = \exttype[\Delta']{S}$, resulting in a new existential type $\delta = \exttype[\Delta'']{S'}$ and a substitution $\phi$ mapping type variables from $\Delta'$
to types with variables in $\Delta''$. We then construct a new arrow with domain $\delta$ and range $\phi(T)$.

%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%% BEGIN EXRED FIG %%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%
\begin{figure}[t!]
\centering
\vspace*{.5em}

\newjudge{Existential Reduction}{\jtreds{\delta}{\delta}{\phi}}
\infrule
  {\jcnequiv{T}{\Bottom}{\C} \andalso \toConstraint{\Delta'}{\C'} \\
   \jsolve{\C \wedge \C'}{\phi}{\C''} \andalso \toBounds{\C''}{\Delta''}}
  {\jtreds{\exttype[\Delta']{T}}{\exttype[\Delta'']{\phi(T)}}{\phi}}
